references.text: Laying hands on the head of the sacrificial animal is also required for peace offerings, showing that this was a standard ritual act to identify the offerer with the sacrifice.
For sin offerings, the hand is also placed on the animal's head before it is slaughtered, emphasizing that laying on of hands was central to atonement rituals.
On the Day of Atonement, Aaron places both hands on the scapegoat and confesses the people's sins, demonstrating the transfer of sin onto the sacrificial animal.
Explains that blood makes atonement for the soul, expanding on the meaning of לְכַפֵּר (to make atonement) mentioned in Leviticus 1:4.
At the consecration of priests, Aaron and his sons were to lay their hands on the head of the bull, showing that laying on of hands was an established practice even before Leviticus.
The Israelites laid their hands on the Levites when they were set apart for service, demonstrating that laying on of hands was also used in the consecration of persons.
Hebrews explains that almost everything is cleansed with blood according to the law, and without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness – this expands on the atonement theology from Leviticus.
Explains that blood from bulls and goats cannot take away sins, pointing forward to Christ's perfect sacrifice as the fulfillment of atonement offerings.
Paul uses the same term for atonement (ἱλαστήριον) regarding Christ, showing how the Old Testament atonement offering points forward to Christ's work.
The ritual act (laying on of hands) and the place of slaughter are identical for the burnt offering and the sin offering, emphasizing a common foundation for atonement.
Confirms that laying on of hands and slaughter at the place of the burnt offering are shared by both burnt and sin offerings, illustrating the role of the sacrifice as a substitute.
Shows how the burnt offering is also used in the highest atonement ritual to make atonement for both the priest and the people, expanding the understanding of the sacrifice's function.
Complements the source verse by showing the conclusion of the process: that the atonement begun with laying on of hands is completed through burning and results in forgiveness.
Confirms that laying hands on the head of the sacrificial animal and slaughtering at the altar is the fixed method for transferring guilt in all sin offering cases.
Highlights the theological purpose of laying on of hands: that the act leads to concrete atonement and forgiveness for the one who has sinned.
